summary: Suggests a method for workstations to access mail dynamically from a mailbox server. It is a modified version of the IMAP2 definition in RFC 1064 and was published as an Experimental protocol. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary:
IMAP3 changes where mail lives: the server holds the mailbox and the workstation only reads it, so the same mailbox can be reached from any machine and all the state stays on the server.

It also fixes a confusion in the earlier version by saying exactly which server messages answer a client request and which the server sends on its own.

questions: how is imap3 different from imap2
what are solicited and unsolicited responses in imap
how does imap tag commands and responses
subtitle: The third version of IMAP, which made the server rather than the workstation the holder of the mailbox.

tldr.problem: IMAP2 was not powerful enough for the server and client interactions the authors wanted, and the competing RFC 1176 added optional features with no way for a client to discover what a server actually supported.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP3 defines tagged commands, a clear split between solicited and unsolicited server data, a server-side search facility, a way to negotiate protocol versions and features, and a model of the mailbox as a set of keys into values.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was written as a counter-proposal to RFC 1176 and superseded RFC 1064. It has not been obsoleted and is Historic.

today: RFC 1203 is a Historic document from February 1991 and has not been obsoleted. It superseded RFC 1064, the IMAP2 definition, and was written as a counter-proposal to RFC 1176.

sections.title: Why IMAP3
sections.content:
The document is a modified version of RFC 1064, the definition of the IMAP2 protocol, written specifically as a counter-proposal to RFC 1176, which itself proposed modifications to IMAP2. The RFC explains that 1176 was made without internal consultation with the IMAP community, so the authors felt they had to present a counter-proposal to something that would otherwise become a de facto standard. The reasons given are that IMAP2 is insufficiently powerful for a number of server and client interactions the authors believe important, that RFC 1176 negligibly enhances that functionality, that IMAP2 makes what the authors consider an erroneous definition of unsolicited against solicited data, and that RFC 1176 specifies optional features with no metaprotocol by which servers and clients can negotiate over the set of implemented features.

The revision tried to make upwards compatible changes wherever possible, but some places had to change incompatibly to compensate for ambiguities in IMAP2 as defined by RFC 1064, or for behaviour that proved undesirable in practice. The goal was still that existing IMAP2 clients should be supported and that, at least for the foreseeable future, all IMAP3 servers would support IMAP2 behaviour as their default mode.

The major differences are listed in the RFC. IMAP3 distinguishes solicited from unsolicited data sent by the server: data required as the result of a request is solicited and carries the tag of the request that provoked it, while data the protocol does not require is unsolicited and carries the special tag *. RFC 1176 keeps the original RFC 1064 terminology and calls all server data unsolicited even when it is in fact solicited. IMAP3 introduces the experimental concept of generic, canonical and concrete keys, which lets the mailbox be viewed as a relational database indexed by those keys and lets the protocol move away from its reliance on RFC 822. The SEARCH command is changed to allow multiple simultaneous searches and unsolicited search messages, which is what lets a server process commands asynchronously over slow storage. IMAP3 introduces a specific protocol for negotiating protocol versions and server features, so that a client and server can agree on what behaviour is really available. It also introduces a mechanism for clients to create and delete user flags, which neither RFC 1176 nor RFC 1064 supported. And because RFC 1064 had no mechanism for determining whether a mailbox was read-only, IMAP3 adds specific protocol additions for the dynamic determination and modification of that status.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP3 is the third attempt at the same idea, and it exists partly because two other proposals were in circulation at once. Its changes are mostly about telling the client clearly what the server can do, and about telling apart answers from announcements.

sections.title: Why the Server Holds the Mailbox
sections.content:
The intent of IMAP3 is to allow a possibly unreliable workstation or similar machine to access electronic mail from a reliable mailbox server in an efficient manner. Although different in many ways from POP2, IMAP3 may be thought of as a functional superset of POP2, and the POP2 RFC was used as a model. Like POP2, IMAP3 specifies a means of accessing stored mail and not of posting mail; posting is handled by a mail transfer protocol such as SMTP.

The system model explains why the server holds the mailbox. With mainframes, each user tends to receive and process mail at the machine used most of the time. Putting an independent workstation in front of a user leads to several disadvantages. Workstations give the user full control at the console, so background tasks such as receiving mail could be prevented from running, leading to repeated failed delivery attempts by outside agents. The hardware failure of a single workstation could keep its user off the air, since repair might be delayed, while a centralised mainframe is generally repaired soon after failure. It is harder to keep track of mailing addresses when each person is associated with a distinct machine, and the host concept suited a time when most organisations had only one central host. And it is very difficult to keep a multitude of heterogeneous workstations working properly with complex mailing protocols as new standards emerge, with each system having to deal with receiving, routing, delivering, formatting, storing and the stability of mailboxes.

So while the workstation may be viewed as an Internet host, it should not be viewed as the entity holding the user's mailbox. A mail server machine, sometimes called a repository, holds the mailbox, and the workstation accesses it through mail transactions. Because the server is isolated from direct user manipulation it can achieve high software reliability easily and, as a shared resource, high hardware reliability, perhaps through redundancy. The server can be used from arbitrary locations, the same user may access the mailbox from different clients at different times, and multiple users may access the same mailbox simultaneously.

The mail server acts as an interface among users, data storage and other mailers. The mail access protocol is used to retrieve messages, access and change properties of messages, and manage mailboxes, and it is used for all message manipulation, isolating the user and the client from any knowledge of how the data storage is used. The RFC also stresses that the client and server form a macrosystem in which the strong points of both can be exploited while compensating for each other's weaknesses, and that IMAP3 has extensive features for remote searching and parsing of messages on the server, so a client can search a whole mailbox without transferring it, and can use the server's structured envelope representation to display envelope information and reply without understanding RFC 822 header parsing at all.

The RFC contrasts this with the DMSP protocol of PCMAIL, where the client and server have a long-term relationship and the client keeps a set of descriptors summarising each message, with the two sides synchronising their state when the connection starts and the client doing a complete reset if it has not connected for a while. In IMAP the relationship lasts only for the duration of the connection, all mailbox state stays on the server, there is no registration of clients, and the function of a descriptor is handled by the structured envelope. IMAP has flag names, with 5 system flag names defined and a facility for some number of user flag names, 29 in the current implementations, where DMSP has 16 binary flags of which 8 are defined by the system.

One crucial philosophical difference is that IMAP is a mailbox access protocol, not a protocol for manipulating mail files. No specification is made for the implementation architecture for mail storage, and servers may implement mailboxes as files without the client being aware. Mailboxes are viewed as mappings from keys into values, in three broad types. Generic keys are mail-format independent and defined by IMAP, such as TO, which would be associated with the To: field of an RFC 822 message. Canonical keys represent the way the server can associate values generally about a key concept, possibly integrating several format-specific fields; the canonical $TO key could denote anything reasonably construed as being directed towards someone, so in an RFC 822 message the server could find the union of the To:, Resent-To:, Apparently-To: and Cc: fields. Concrete keys let the client reach mail-format specific concepts that IMAP does not pre-specify, so a request for APPARENTLY-TO would look for a header field of that name in an RFC 822 message, and the server responds with the null value NIL if there is no such field or it is not meaningful for that message format.
sections.plainLanguage: The server keeps the mail and the client only reads it. That way the mail is not lost when a workstation breaks, and the mailbox is the same wherever you read it from. The server also presents each message as a set of named fields, so the client does not have to understand the RFC 822 header format.

sections.title: How the Protocol Works
sections.content:
The IMAP3 protocol consists of a sequence of client commands and server responses to those commands, with extra information from the server sent asynchronously and independently of the responses to client commands. Unlike most Internet protocols, commands and responses are tagged: a command begins with a unique identifier, typically a short alphanumeric sequence such as A0001 or A0002, and the response to that command carries the same tag from the server.

Data sent by the server as the result of a client request is called SOLICITED and is identified by the tag of the initial request. Data sent by the server not as the result of a client request is called UNSOLICITED and carries the reserved tag *. The server may send unsolicited data at any time that would not fragment another piece of data on the same stream. The server is contractually required to return all solicited data before the completion signal for that command, so the client can be confident that it has everything it asked for when the request finishes. This does not preclude simultaneous processing of multiple requests, so both synchronous and asynchronous clients can be implemented. No assumptions about serial or monolithic processing by the server can be made by a correct client, since the server is at liberty to process multiple requests in any order, which lets it run costly searches in the background while preserving interactive performance.

When a connection is opened the server sends an unsolicited OK response as a greeting and then waits for commands. The client opens a connection, waits for the greeting, sends a LOGIN command with user name and password to establish authorisation, and after an OK response sends a SELECT command to access the desired mailbox. The default mailbox has the reserved name INBOX, which is independent of the operating system the server runs on. The server generally sends a list of valid flags, the number of messages and the number of messages arrived since the last access as solicited data, followed by an OK response. Because SELECT changes the state of the server fundamentally, the server must process all outstanding commands for the mailbox before sending the OK tag, so the client always knows which mailbox the surrounding responses refer to.

Because local needs and experimental work will dictate servers that support both supersets of the defined behaviour and incompatible changes, servers support a SELECT.VERSION command and a SELECT.FEATURES command, letting clients select the overall behaviour and specific features they want. The default behaviour of any server is the interaction syntax specified by IMAP2 in RFC 1064, and a server may not behave in any other manner unless SELECT.VERSION or SELECT.FEATURES is used. The version numbers denote versions of the IMAP protocol, not of the server, so a client should not rely on tests of the form if major_version is greater than 2 being valid for all protocol versions.

The client reads mailbox information with FETCH commands, which should be viewed as poking the server to include the desired data along with any other data it wishes to transmit. The client alters certain data with STORE, and a message is deleted from a mailbox by a STORE command that includes the DELETED flag among the flags being set. Other operations include COPY to copy a message to another mailbox, EXPUNGE to permanently remove deleted messages, CHECK to check for new messages, and SEARCH to find messages matching criteria. The client ends the session with LOGOUT, and the server returns a BYE followed by an OK.
sections.plainLanguage: Every command carries a number, and every answer to it carries the same number back, so the client can match them up. The server may also send messages the client did not ask for, and those carry a reserved tag instead.

sections.title: Data Items, Flags and Search Criteria
sections.content:
There are three major categories of data that may be fetched. The first is data associated with a message as an entity in the mailbox, of which there are presently three items: the internal date, meaning the date and time the message was placed in the mailbox; the RFC 822 size, the size in bytes of the message expressed as an RFC 822 text string, which is subject to deletion in the future and which current clients use only in a status display line; and the flags, a list of status flags associated with the message. All of this first category can be fetched with the macro-fetch word FAST, which expands to (FLAGS INTERNALDATE RFC822.SIZE).

The second category describes the composition and delivery information of a message, such as the sender, the recipient lists, the message ID and the subject. This is the information stored in the message header of an RFC 822 message and is traditionally called the envelope, which should not be confused with the SMTP envelope, which is strictly limited to delivery information. IMAP3 defines a structured and unambiguous representation for the envelope, which is particularly nice for Lisp-based parsers, so a client can use it for operations such as replying without worrying about RFC 822 at all. The first and second categories can be fetched together with the macro-fetch word ALL, which expands to (FLAGS INTERNALDATE RFC822.SIZE ENVELOPE).

The third category is data intended for direct human viewing. The present RFC 822 based IMAP3 defines three such items: RFC822.HEADER, RFC822.TEXT, and RFC822, which is the two former appended together in a single text string. Fetching RFC822 is equivalent to typing the RFC 822 representation of the message as stored on the mailbox without any filtering or processing. Typically a client fetches ALL for some or all of the messages in the mailbox for use as a presentation menu, and fetches RFC822.TEXT when the user wishes to read a particular message. A more primitive client could simply fetch RFC822, POP2-style.

The predefined generic keys are BCC, BODY, CC, FROM, HEADER, SIZE, SUBJECT, TEXT and TO, and the predefined canonical keys are $CC, $FROM, $SUBJECT and $TO. The value returned for a non-existent or non-meaningful key is the null value, NIL. The system flags are RECENT, meaning the message arrived since the last read of the mailbox; SEEN, meaning the message has been read; ANSWERED, meaning it has been answered; FLAGGED, meaning it is flagged for urgent or special attention; and DELETED, meaning it is marked for removal by a later EXPUNGE.

The SEARCH command searches the mailbox for messages that match the given criteria, and the response gives the set of messages matching the conjunction of the criteria. Each criterion has a logical inverse, written with a tilde, so a message matching FROM crispin does not match ~FROM crispin. Besides the generic, canonical and concrete keys, the predefined criteria include ALL, ANSWERED, BCC, BEFORE, BODY, CC, DELETED, FLAGGED, FROM, HEADER, KEYWORD, NEW, OLD, ON, RECENT, SEEN, SINCE, SUBJECT, TEXT and TO. The older UNANSWERED, UNDELETED, UNFLAGGED, UNKEYWORD and UNSEEN criteria are preserved for IMAP2 compatibility but are considered obsolete, and new client programs are encouraged to use the tilde notation instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask for three kinds of thing about a message: facts about the message itself such as its size and date, the envelope of who it came from and what it is about, or the raw text for display. Searches run on the server over the whole mailbox.

sections.title: A Typical Session
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a typical session. The client opens the connection and receives the unsolicited greeting * OK IMAP3 Server Ready. It then asks what the server supports with A001 SUPPORTED.VERSIONS, and the server replies with the versions it knows, listing 2 0 and 3 0 together with the features EIGHT.BIT.TRANSPARENT, AUTO.SET.SEEN and TAGGED.SOLICITED, followed by A001 OK Supported Versions returned.

The client selects version 3.0 with A002 SELECT.VERSION (3 0), which the server confirms with A002 OK Version 3.0 Selected, and then selects the features it wants with A002 SELECT.FEATURES TAGGED.SOLICITED. It logs in with A003 LOGIN Fred Secret and gets A003 OK User Fred logged in, then selects the mailbox with A004 SELECT INBOX. The server sends back the flags applicable to that mailbox, Meeting Notice, Answered, Flagged, Deleted and Seen, then A004 19 EXISTS, A004 2 RECENT and A004 OK Select complete.

The client fetches the headers of the whole mailbox with A005 FETCH 1:19 ALL, and the server returns a Fetch response for each of the nineteen messages followed by A005 OK Fetch complete. When the user wants to read one message, the client sends A006 FETCH 8 RFC822.TEXT and the server returns the 893 characters of text, followed by A006 OK Fetch complete. The client then marks that message for deletion with A007 STORE 8 +Flags Deleted, and the server replies with the resulting flag set, Deleted and Seen, and A007 OK Store complete. The client removes the deleted messages permanently with A008 EXPUNGE, and the server reports the message count dropping to 18, A008 8 EXPUNGE, and then 18 EXISTS. Finally the client sends A009 LOGOUT, and the server answers A009 BYE IMAP3 server quitting followed by A009 OK Logout complete before closing the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A session runs like this: log in, choose a mailbox, fetch what you need, change flags as you read, and log out. The numbers on each line match the command to its answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of RFC 1203 says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The protocol itself has one thing to say about authorisation: the LOGIN command identifies the user to the server and carries the password authenticating that user, and this information is used by the server to control access to the mailboxes. The server must also check that the user is permitted read access to a mailbox before returning an OK to a SELECT, and it reports a mailbox as read-only when the user cannot write to it.
sections.plainLanguage: This document has almost nothing to say about security. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed here, and the password handling it does describe is in the LOGIN command.
